newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Mideast tops agenda of EU foreign ministers.
newsitem.headline: Mideast tops agenda of EU foreign ministers.

text.p: Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring said on Friday that the Middle East peace process and former Yugoslavia would be the main focus of an informal weekend meeting of European foreign ministers.
Spring, whose country current holds the presidency of the European Union, said sharply differing views among EU states about U.S. attacks on Iraq would also be aired.
"The main focus, from my point of view, will be the Middle East peace process and former Yugoslavia," Spring told Reuters in Tralee, southern Ireland, where the talks start on Saturday.
Carl Bildt, the EU's Bosnia envoy, will brief ministers on the buildup to September 14 elections which are seen as a test of international efforts to restore normality to Bosnia after the war.
Spring, who takes a keen interest in the Middle East, held talks with Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy on Thursday night and will brief his EU counterparts on the discussions over the weekend.
The EU is anxious that the new right-wing Israeli government show the same commitment to the peace process as its predecessor.

Levy, on a European tour, paid a courtesty call on Irish Prime Minister John Bruton in Dublin on Friday and was later flying to London. After meeting Bruton he told reporters he did not expect criticism of Israel's handling of the peace process to emerge from the EU meeting.

"I feel that there is a wish in Europe prevailing to see the (peace) process continuing and advancing," Levy said. "When both sides reach an agreement I think that friendly countries like the European countries would give their blessing to it."
President Bill Clinton's punitive attacks on Iraq for an incursion into Kurdish areas have failed to win wholehearted support in the 15-nation bloc.
France, an enthusiastic supporter of Washington during the 1991 Gulf war, has expressed reservations about the attack, arguing that Saddam's forces were invited into the area by a Kurdish faction.
It has not supported Washington's extension of a no-fly zone in southern Iraq, where much of Saddam's troops, planes and radar equipment are based.
But other states, notably Britain, have thrown their weight behind Clinton's policies, exposing rifts among America's key allies about how to deal with Saddam.

"Certainly there are widely differing views on Iraq but I don't expect it to dominate the agenda, but certainly it will be discussed," said Spring, whose own country's reaction to the U.S. raids has been muted.

Spring said the other main topic of the discussions would be relations between the United States and the EU, which have been strained by Washington's decision to punish companies trading with Cuba, Libya and Iran.
The EU has threatened to take U.S. sanctions against Cuba, which it sees as an application of U.S. laws in a foreign country, to the World Trade Organisation.
Spring said ministers would also review the outcome of Russian elections which returned an ailing Boris Yeltsin to power.
The two-day talks begin at midday on Saturday and end on Sunday afternoon.
